entries.meaning: To buy and sell a particular kind of goods, or to include someone in a card game or a scheme.
examples: The gallery deals in nineteenth-century prints.
His family dealt in grain for a century.
That website deals in rumor more than news.
Deal me in — I've got twenty bucks.
She dealt the new guy in on the second hand.
If there's money in it, deal us in.

senses.head: Trade in, buy and sell
body: Of a business and the goods it handles, and figuratively of what a person or a paper traffics in. In here is a preposition, so nothing can come between the two words. (торговать чем-либо)
examples: The gallery deals in nineteenth-century prints.
His family dealt in grain for a century.
That website deals in rumor more than news.

senses.head: Include someone in the game
body: From the card table, and extended to any scheme with money in it. Here in is a particle and the person always sits in front of it. (включить в игру, взять в долю)
examples: Deal me in — I've got twenty bucks.
She dealt the new guy in on the second hand.
If there's money in it, deal us in.

entries.pronunciation note: in the trade sense in is a preposition and deal keeps the stress; in the card sense it is a true particle and takes the stress — deal me IN
entries.русский: торговать (чем-л.); включить в игру, взять в долю
entries.type: prepositional verb (verb + preposition) in the trade sense; phrasal verb (verb + particle) in the card sense
entries.separable: it depends on the sense. Trading: no — the gallery deals in prints, ✗ deals prints in, ✗ deals it in. Cards: yes, and the object always separates — deal me in, deal the new guy in, never ✗ deal in me.
entries.transitive: yes — a commodity in the trade sense, a person in the card sense
entries.register: everyday — plain business talk, and deal me in is plain speech
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: the habitual trade sense (the gallery deals in prints) and the one-time card sense (deal me in). No linking or stative use.
entries.passive: restricted — the card sense passivizes: I was dealt in on the second hand. The trade sense barely does: ✗ nineteenth-century prints are dealt in by the gallery.
entries.see also: deal out, deal with, do out of

entries.meaning: To hand something out portion by portion, especially cards, or to hand out punishment.
examples: He dealt out five cards to each player.
Deal them out and let's play.
The estate was dealt out among four cousins.
Judges here deal out the same sentence for a first offense.
The coach deals criticism out freely and takes none.
Whatever the league deals out, they'll appeal it.

senses.head: Distribute in portions
body: Cards first of all, and by extension shares, supplies, or anything divided among people. (раздавать, распределять)
examples: He dealt out five cards to each player.
Deal them out and let's play.
The estate was dealt out among four cousins.

senses.head: Administer punishment or justice
body: The object is a sentence, a penalty, or criticism. Slightly formal, and common in court reporting. (вершить, назначать наказание)
examples: Judges here deal out the same sentence for a first offense.
The coach deals criticism out freely and takes none.
Whatever the league deals out, they'll appeal it.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, which is what makes the two words sound like one verb
entries.separable: yes — deal out the cards / deal the cards out, and with a pronoun it must separate: deal them out, never ✗ deal out them.
entries.register: everyday — the card sense is plain speech; the punishment sense sounds slightly formal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: handing out cards or portions, and administering a penalty. Progressive is normal — he's dealing out the cards.
entries.passive: yes — the estate was dealt out among four cousins; the same sentence is dealt out for a first offense.
entries.see also: deal in, deal with, drive home

entries.meaning: To handle a problem or a person, to do business with someone, or — of a text — to be about a subject.
examples: I deal with vendor complaints all morning.
He dealt with the same landlord for six years.
I can't deal with her today.
We only deal with suppliers who deliver on time.
The claim has already been dealt with by their office.
Chapter four deals with the war years.
The report dealt with only one of the three sites.

senses.head: Handle, cope with
body: The core sense. The object is a problem, a complaint, or a difficult person. (справляться с, разбираться с)
examples: I deal with vendor complaints all morning.
He dealt with the same landlord for six years.
I can't deal with her today.

senses.head: Do business with
body: Of the companies and people you transact with regularly. (иметь дело с, сотрудничать)
examples: We only deal with suppliers who deliver on time.
The claim has already been dealt with by their office.

senses.head: Be about (of a text)
body: Of books, chapters, reports, and laws: what the text covers. (быть посвящённым, рассматривать)
examples: Chapter four deals with the war years.
The report dealt with only one of the three sites.

entries.pronunciation note: with is a preposition, so deal keeps the stress; it never becomes ✗ deel-WITH
entries.русский: иметь дело с, разбираться с; быть посвящённым (теме)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows with. ✗ deal the complaint with, ✗ deal it with. Only the passive moves the object out front: the complaint was dealt with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the handling and business senses (I'm dealing with vendor complaints), but stative in the be-about sense: ✗ chapter four is dealing with the war years.
entries.passive: restricted — full prepositional passive in the handling and business senses: the complaint has already been dealt with. The be-about sense resists it: ✗ the war years are dealt with by chapter four.
entries.see also: deal in, do away with, put up with

entries.meaning: To start eating, to entrench yourself, or to refuse to move from a position.
examples: Everybody grab a plate and dig in.
The kids dug in before I sat down.
The battalion dug in along the ridge and waited.
Management has dug in and won't reopen the contract.
She dug her heels in and refused to sign.
Once he digs in his heels, no argument moves him.

senses.head: Start eating
body: Nearly always the bare imperative, said over a table of food. (приниматься за еду, налетать)
examples: Everybody grab a plate and dig in.
The kids dug in before I sat down.

senses.head: Entrench, take a defensive position
body: Military first, then figurative: a side that will not move. (окапываться; занять жёсткую позицию)
examples: The battalion dug in along the ridge and waited.
Management has dug in and won't reopen the contract.

senses.head: Dig in one's heels
body: A fixed idiom for refusing to budge. The object is always heels, and it can sit on either side of the particle. (упереться, стоять на своём)
examples: She dug her heels in and refused to sign.
Once he digs in his heels, no argument moves him.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — dig IN, not DIG in
entries.русский: приниматься за еду; окапываться; упереться, стоять на своём
entries.separable: usually there is nothing to separate, because the verb takes no object. The one object it does take is heels, in the idiom, and there both orders work — dig in your heels / dig your heels in.
entries.transitive: usually no; the one object it takes is heels, in the idiom
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: starting to eat, entrenching, and the dig in one's heels idiom. Progressive is normal — management has been digging in for weeks.
entries.passive: no — the eating and entrenching senses take no object at all, and the one object it does take resists the passive: ✗ her heels were dug in.
entries.see also: dig into, dig out, eat up

entries.meaning: To investigate something thoroughly, to start eating something with appetite, or to draw on a reserve.
examples: Reporters dug into his campaign filings.
I dug into the logs and found the bug in an hour.
She has been digging into the family's history for years.
He dug into a plate of ribs without a word.
We had to dig into savings to cover the repair.

senses.head: Investigate
body: The reporter's and the engineer's word for looking past the surface of a record, a dataset, or a story. (копаться в, вникать в)
examples: Reporters dug into his campaign filings.
I dug into the logs and found the bug in an hour.
She has been digging into the family's history for years.

senses.head: Start eating with appetite
body: Of a plate of food in front of you. (налечь на, приниматься за)
examples: He dug into a plate of ribs without a word.

senses.head: Draw on a reserve
body: Of savings, a fund, or a margin you were trying not to touch. (залезть в, потратить часть)
examples: We had to dig into savings to cover the repair.

entries.pronunciation note: into is a preposition, so dig keeps the stress; compare the true particle in dig UP
entries.русский: копаться в, вникать в; налечь на (еду); залезть в (сбережения)
entries.separable: no — dig into the records, ✗ dig the records into, ✗ dig it into. Pronouns follow the preposition: dig into it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: investigating, tucking into food, drawing on savings. Progressive is common — she has been digging into the family's history.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is marginal even in the investigate sense: ?his campaign filings were dug into for weeks. None at all in the food and savings senses: ✗ savings were dug into.
entries.see also: dig up, dig out, eat into

entries.meaning: To find something that was stored away and forgotten, or to free something buried.
examples: I'll dig out the warranty and email it to you.
She dug her old resume out of a drawer.
Can you dig them out before the meeting?
Crews dug two cars out of the drift.
It took the town a week to dig itself out.

senses.head: Retrieve something put away
body: Of papers, clothes, files — anything you have to go looking for. (откопать, разыскать)
examples: I'll dig out the warranty and email it to you.
She dug her old resume out of a drawer.
Can you dig them out before the meeting?

senses.head: Free from snow or rubble
body: Literal, and the standard word after a blizzard. (откапывать, расчищать)
examples: Crews dug two cars out of the drift.
It took the town a week to dig itself out.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — dig it OUT
entries.русский: откопать, разыскать; выкопать, откапывать из-под снега
entries.separable: yes — dig out the old photos / dig the old photos out, and with a pronoun it must separate: dig them out, never ✗ dig out them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: retrieving something stored away, and freeing something buried.
entries.passive: yes — the warranty was dug out and emailed over; two cars were dug out of the drift.
entries.see also: dig up, dig into, find out

entries.meaning: To uncover information someone would rather keep buried, or to remove something from the ground.
examples: Opposition researchers dug up an old lawsuit.
The paper dug the whole story up two weeks before the vote.
If there's dirt, they'll dig it up.
The defense dug up a witness nobody had talked to.
We dug up the yard looking for the leak.

senses.head: Unearth facts
body: Of the damaging kind, usually. This is the verb behind opposition research. (раскопать, разузнать)
examples: Opposition researchers dug up an old lawsuit.
The paper dug the whole story up two weeks before the vote.
If there's dirt, they'll dig it up.

senses.head: Produce something with effort
body: Of a witness, a document, a spare part — something found only by looking hard. (раздобыть, откопать)
examples: The defense dug up a witness nobody had talked to.

senses.head: Remove from the ground
body: The literal sense, of yards, roads, and plants. (выкопать, перекопать)
examples: We dug up the yard looking for the leak.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — dig it UP
entries.separable: yes — dig up dirt on him / dig the dirt up, and with a pronoun it must separate: dig it up, never ✗ dig up it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: unearthing facts, producing something with effort, or turning over ground.
entries.passive: yes — an old lawsuit was dug up by opposition researchers; the whole yard was dug up looking for the leak.
entries.see also: dig out, dig into, find out

entries.meaning: To abolish something, or — older and jokier — to kill someone.
examples: The city did away with paper permits last year.
They want to do away with the whole department.
Nobody's going to do away with it before the election.
The rule has been done away with twice and brought back twice.
In the last chapter somebody does away with the butler.

senses.head: Abolish, get rid of
body: Of rules, fees, offices, and practices. Slightly more formal than get rid of, and the standard verb in news writing. (отменить, упразднить)
examples: The city did away with paper permits last year.
They want to do away with the whole department.
Nobody's going to do away with it before the election.
The rule has been done away with twice and brought back twice.

senses.head: Kill
body: Dated and euphemistic, and now mostly a joke or a detective-story line. (прикончить, устранить)
examples: In the last chapter somebody does away with the butler.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on away, not on do and not on with
entries.separable: no — ordinary three-part verbs never split. do away with the fee, ✗ do the fee away with, ✗ do it away with. Pronouns go at the end: do away with it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both the abolish sense and the dated kill sense. Progressive is fine — they're doing away with paper permits.
entries.passive: yes, and the entry shows it — the rule has been done away with twice and brought back twice. The particle chain stays intact after the verb.
entries.see also: do without, do in, forget about

entries.meaning: To exhaust, ruin, or finish someone or something off.
examples: That last hill just about did for me.
Two winters in that apartment did for the pipes.
Another season like this one would do for the team.
If the bank calls the loan, we're done for.
He knew from her face that he was done for.

senses.head: Wear out or destroy
body: British and old-fashioned in the active. (доконать, погубить)
examples: That last hill just about did for me.
Two winters in that apartment did for the pipes.
Another season like this one would do for the team.

senses.head: Be done for
body: The fixed participle, and the only form Americans use: finished, doomed, with no hope left. (пропал, конец)
examples: If the bank calls the loan, we're done for.
He knew from her face that he was done for.

entries.pronunciation note: for is a preposition, so do keeps the stress
entries.separable: no — that hill did for me, ✗ did me for. The object always follows the preposition.
entries.register: British — the active verb is British and dated; American English keeps only the participle, done for, meaning finished or doomed
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the British active sense (that hill did for me); the American survival, be done for, is a fixed participle used adjectivally, i.e. stative.
entries.passive: restricted — no true passive of the active verb (✗ the pipes were done for by two winters). Only the adjectival participle lives on: if the bank calls the loan, we're done for.
entries.see also: do in, do over, wear out

entries.meaning: To exhaust someone completely, or to kill someone.
examples: Three flights of stairs did me in.
The heat did in half the crew by noon.
I'm done in — I'm going to bed.
Somebody did the witness in before the trial.
He swore the cold weather would do him in eventually.

senses.head: Wear out, exhaust
body: Most often with a pronoun object, or in the participle done in. (вымотать, доконать)
examples: Three flights of stairs did me in.
The heat did in half the crew by noon.
I'm done in — I'm going to bed.

senses.head: Kill
body: Crime-novel informal, never used in a report or a news story. (прикончить, убрать)
examples: Somebody did the witness in before the trial.
He swore the cold weather would do him in eventually.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — it did me IN
entries.separable: yes, and with a pronoun it must separate: that hike did me in, never ✗ did in me. With a full noun both orders work: the flu did in half the office / did half the office in.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, exhausting someone and killing someone. The participle done in also serves as an adjective: I'm done in.
entries.passive: yes — the witness was done in before the trial; half the crew was done in by the heat.
entries.see also: do for, do up, wear out

entries.meaning: To cheat someone out of something they were owed.
examples: The contractor did them out of a month's pay.
She says her brother did her out of her share of the house.
That parking ticket did me out of a night at the movies.
They'd done the old man out of his savings years before.
Don't let a technicality do you out of the refund.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on out, the particle, not on do
entries.separable: yes, and it must be — this is the one three-part verb on the page that splits. The person cheated always sits between do and out of, and the thing lost follows: they did her out of her commission, they did me out of it. ✗ do out of her the commission, ✗ do out of her her commission.
entries.transitive: yes, two objects — the person cheated and the thing lost
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of cheating someone. Progressive is fine — they're doing her out of her share.
entries.passive: yes, with the person cheated as subject — she was done out of her share of the house. The thing lost cannot front: ✗ her commission was done her out of.
entries.see also: do in, do over, find out

entries.meaning: To do something again from the start, or to redecorate a room.
examples: The whole page was wrong, so I did it over.
She made him do the essay over.
If I could do this year over, I would.
They did over the kitchen in the spring.
Their flat got done over while they were away.

senses.head: Redo from the start
body: The everyday American sense, and the source of the schoolyard noun a do-over. (переделать заново)
examples: The whole page was wrong, so I did it over.
She made him do the essay over.
If I could do this year over, I would.

senses.head: Redecorate
body: Of a room or a house given a new look. (отделать заново, переделать интерьер)
examples: They did over the kitchen in the spring.

senses.head: Burgle or beat up
body: British and informal, and a false friend for Americans. (обчистить; отделать, избить)
examples: Their flat got done over while they were away.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — do it OVER
entries.separable: yes — do over the whole kitchen / do the whole kitchen over, and with a pronoun it must separate: do it over, never ✗ do over it.
entries.register: everyday — do it over is the standard American way to say redo; British do over, meaning burgle or beat up, is a separate informal verb
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: redoing a task, redecorating a room, and British burgling or beating up.
entries.passive: yes — the essay had to be done over; the kitchen was done over in the spring; their flat got done over while they were away.
entries.see also: do up, do in, fit up

entries.meaning: To fasten something, to wrap it, or to fix a place up.
examples: Do up your coat, it's freezing.
He couldn't do his tie up straight.
The laces are loose — do them up.
She did the package up in brown paper.
They bought a wreck and did it up over two summers.
She showed up done up like it was a wedding.

senses.head: Fasten
body: Of buttons, zippers, laces, and ties. The opposite is undo. (застегнуть, завязать)
examples: Do up your coat, it's freezing.
He couldn't do his tie up straight.
The laces are loose — do them up.

senses.head: Wrap or package
body: Of parcels and presents. (упаковать, завернуть)
examples: She did the package up in brown paper.

senses.head: Renovate, or dress up
body: Of a run-down house, and of a person turned out for an occasion — all done up. (отремонтировать; принарядиться)
examples: They bought a wreck and did it up over two summers.
She showed up done up like it was a wedding.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — do it UP
entries.separable: yes — do up your coat / do your coat up, and with a pronoun it must separate: do it up, never ✗ do up it.
entries.register: everyday — the fastening sense is commoner in British English; Americans more often say button up or zip up
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: fastening, wrapping, renovating. The participle done up doubles as an adjective — she showed up done up like it was a wedding.
entries.passive: yes — the package was done up in brown paper; the house was done up over two summers.
entries.see also: do over, fit out, draw up

entries.meaning: To need or want something, in could do with, or to be connected with something, in have to do with.
examples: I could do with a cup of coffee.
This room could do with a coat of paint.
The delay has nothing to do with the weather.
What does any of this have to do with me?
She didn't know what to do with herself all afternoon.

senses.head: Could do with
body: A mild way of saying you need something. Common in both American and British speech, though the British use it more. (пригодиться, не помешало бы)
examples: I could do with a cup of coffee.
This room could do with a coat of paint.

senses.head: Have to do with
body: Be connected to, be about. Almost always in this fixed frame. (иметь отношение к)
examples: The delay has nothing to do with the weather.
What does any of this have to do with me?

senses.head: What to do with
body: How to handle a thing, a problem, or yourself. (как поступить с)
examples: She didn't know what to do with herself all afternoon.

entries.pronunciation note: with is a preposition, so do keeps the stress
entries.русский: пригодиться, не помешало бы; иметь отношение к
entries.separable: no — I could do with a break, ✗ do a break with, ✗ do it with. Pronouns follow the preposition: what did you do with it?
entries.verb type: stative in both fixed frames — could do with is a want or need and have to do with is a relation: ✗ I am doing with a coffee, ✗ the delay is having nothing to do with the weather. Only what to do with is dynamic.
entries.passive: no — both frames are fixed and take no passive: ✗ a cup of coffee could be done with, ✗ the weather is had nothing to do with.
entries.see also: do without, deal with, feel like

entries.meaning: To manage without something you would normally have.
examples: We did without a car for two years.
I can do without the commentary, thanks.
If the store's closed we'll do without.
She's done without worse than this.
You can do without sugar for a week and barely notice.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress lands on the second syllable of without; do is unstressed
entries.separable: no — do without a car, ✗ do a car without, ✗ do it without. It can also stand with no object at all: we'll just have to do without.
entries.transitive: either — with an object, or with none at all
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an ongoing managing rather than a state: we're doing without a car this year is fine. Works with an object or with none at all.
entries.passive: no — ✗ a car was done without for two years. The object stays after the preposition, and the objectless use has nothing to passivize.
entries.see also: do with, do away with, get by

entries.meaning: To move away suddenly, or to pull out of something you had committed to.
examples: She drew back when the dog lunged.
He drew back from the window.
The company drew back from the merger at the last minute.
Two senators have drawn back since the vote was scheduled.
Nobody draws back now without looking scared.

senses.head: Move back physically
body: A recoil — a small, involuntary step away. (отпрянуть, отшатнуться)
examples: She drew back when the dog lunged.
He drew back from the window.

senses.head: Withdraw from a commitment
body: Of a company, a government, or a person losing nerve. Usually with from. (пойти на попятную, отказаться)
examples: The company drew back from the merger at the last minute.
Two senators have drawn back since the vote was scheduled.
Nobody draws back now without looking scared.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — she drew BACK
entries.русский: отпрянуть, отступить; воздержаться, пойти на попятную
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate. When from follows, the phrase still stays whole: drew back from the deal, ✗ drew the deal back from.
entries.register: everyday — the recoil sense is a shade literary; the pulling-out sense is plain business talk
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: the physical recoil and the pulling out of a commitment.
entries.passive: no — the verb takes no object in either sense, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the merger was drawn back from.
entries.see also: draw in, fall back, draw down

entries.meaning: To reduce a stock, a reserve, or a troop level by using it up.
examples: The Fed drew down its emergency facilities over the summer.
They drew the strategic reserve down by forty million barrels.
Once the credit line is open you can draw it down in stages.
The plan draws down troop levels by a third over two years.
Inventories have been drawn down faster than the plants can refill them.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — draw them DOWN
entries.separable: yes — draw down the reserves / draw the reserves down, and with a pronoun it must separate: draw them down, never ✗ draw down them.
entries.transitive: either — usually with an object, but also intransitive in finance: inventories drew down
entries.register: formal — finance, military, and policy writing; in speech the noun drawdown is more common than the verb
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: reducing a reserve by using it. Progressive is standard in finance writing — they're drawing down the credit line in stages.
entries.passive: yes, and the entry shows it — inventories have been drawn down faster than the plants can refill them.
entries.see also: draw on, drive down, draw out

entries.meaning: To attract someone into something, or — of daylight — to shorten.
examples: The window display draws people in off the street.
A free first month drew in thousands of subscribers.
The plot is slow, but it draws you in.
The nights are drawing in already.
The last train drew in just after midnight.

senses.head: Attract, pull someone in
body: Of displays, offers, and stories that catch people and hold them. (привлекать, втягивать)
examples: The window display draws people in off the street.
A free first month drew in thousands of subscribers.
The plot is slow, but it draws you in.

senses.head: Shorten, of the daylight
body: British, said of autumn evenings. (убывать, о дне)
examples: The nights are drawing in already.

senses.head: Arrive, of a train
body: Of a train pulling into a station. Slightly literary in American English. (подходить к перрону)
examples: The last train drew in just after midnight.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — it draws you IN
entries.русский: привлекать, втягивать; (о днях) убывать; подойти к перрону
entries.separable: yes in the attract sense — draw in new customers / draw new customers in, and with a pronoun it must separate: it draws you in, never ✗ draws in you. In the shortening-days and arriving-train senses there is no object at all.
entries.register: everyday — the nights are drawing in sense is British; Americans say the days are getting shorter
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: attracting people, the shortening of daylight, and a train arriving.
entries.passive: yes in the attract sense — thousands of subscribers were drawn in by a free first month. No passive of the daylight or train senses, which take no object.
entries.see also: draw out, draw back, drive away

entries.meaning: To make use of a resource, a fund, or an experience.
examples: The book draws on twenty years of court records.
She drew on her savings to keep the shop open.
We can draw on the emergency fund if we have to.
He drew upon a lifetime of bad decisions for the memoir.
As the evening drew on, fewer people spoke.

senses.head: Make use of
body: Of savings, records, expertise — a store you dip into rather than exhaust. (черпать, использовать)
examples: The book draws on twenty years of court records.
She drew on her savings to keep the shop open.
We can draw on the emergency fund if we have to.
He drew upon a lifetime of bad decisions for the memoir.

senses.head: Approach, of time
body: Of an evening or a season getting late. Literary. (приближаться, клониться к концу)
examples: As the evening drew on, fewer people spoke.

entries.pronunciation note: on is a preposition here, so draw keeps the stress; compare the true particle in draw OUT
entries.separable: no — draw on her experience, ✗ draw her experience on, ✗ draw it on. (Draw on meaning pull clothing on is a different, separable verb: draw the gloves on.)
entries.transitive: yes in the main sense; the time sense takes no object
entries.register: everyday — commonest in writing and in careful speech; draw upon is the more formal variant
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: dipping into a resource (she's drawing on her savings), and in the literary time sense (as the evening drew on).
entries.passive: restricted — the resource sense takes a prepositional passive in careful writing: the emergency fund was drawn on twice that year. The time sense has no object and no passive.
entries.see also: draw down, fall back on, dig into

entries.meaning: To make something last longer than it needs to, to get a quiet person talking, or to withdraw money.
examples: Don't draw the goodbyes out.
The negotiation was drawn out over eleven months.
It's a short story, and he draws it out for two hundred pages.
Her grandmother could draw out the shyest kid in the room.
He drew out three hundred pounds before the banks closed.

senses.head: Prolong
body: Of a meeting, a story, a negotiation — stretched past its natural length. (затягивать, растягивать)
examples: Don't draw the goodbyes out.
The negotiation was drawn out over eleven months.
It's a short story, and he draws it out for two hundred pages.

senses.head: Get someone to open up
body: Of a shy or guarded person coaxed into talking. (разговорить, вызвать на разговор)
examples: Her grandmother could draw out the shyest kid in the room.

senses.head: Withdraw money
body: Chiefly British; Americans say take out or withdraw. (снять деньги со счёта)
examples: He drew out three hundred pounds before the banks closed.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — don't draw it OUT
entries.separable: yes — draw out the meeting / draw the meeting out, and with a pronoun it must separate: draw it out, never ✗ draw out it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: prolonging, coaxing someone into talking, and withdrawing money.
entries.passive: yes, and the entry shows it — the negotiation was drawn out over eleven months; the shyest kid in the room was drawn out.
entries.see also: draw in, draw up, hold up

entries.meaning: To write out a formal document or plan, or — of a vehicle — to pull to a stop.
examples: Our lawyer drew up the lease in an afternoon.
They drew a list up on the back of a receipt.
Send me the terms and I'll draw them up.
A black car drew up outside the courthouse.
He drew himself up and told them to leave.

senses.head: Prepare a document or plan
body: Of contracts, leases, lists, and proposals. The standard verb in legal and office talk. (составлять, оформлять)
examples: Our lawyer drew up the lease in an afternoon.
They drew a list up on the back of a receipt.
Send me the terms and I'll draw them up.

senses.head: Come to a stop
body: Of a car, cab, or carriage pulling in at the curb. (подъехать и остановиться)
examples: A black car drew up outside the courthouse.

senses.head: Draw oneself up
body: To straighten to full height, usually before saying something cutting. (выпрямиться, приосаниться)
examples: He drew himself up and told them to leave.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — draw it UP
entries.separable: yes — draw up a contract / draw the contract up, and with a pronoun it must separate: draw it up, never ✗ draw up it. In the vehicle sense there is no object: a cab drew up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: preparing a document, a vehicle pulling to a stop, or straightening to full height in draw oneself up.
entries.passive: yes in the document sense — the lease was drawn up in an afternoon. No passive of the vehicle sense (no object) or of the reflexive: ✗ he was drawn up by himself.
entries.see also: draw out, do up, fit out

entries.meaning: To long for something, or — in the negative — to refuse even to consider it.
examples: She dreams of a year with nothing scheduled.
He dreamed of playing in the majors until he was twenty.
It's the kind of offer most people only dream of.
I wouldn't dream of charging you for that.
Nobody would have dreamed of asking him directly.

senses.head: Long for, imagine
body: Of a wish rather than a plan. Dream about is the neutral alternative; dream of leans toward longing. (мечтать о)
examples: She dreams of a year with nothing scheduled.
He dreamed of playing in the majors until he was twenty.
It's the kind of offer most people only dream of.

senses.head: Wouldn't dream of
body: A fixed negative meaning I would never consider doing that — usually polite, sometimes indignant. (и в мыслях не иметь, ни за что)
examples: I wouldn't dream of charging you for that.
Nobody would have dreamed of asking him directly.

entries.pronunciation note: of is a preposition, so dream keeps the stress; compare the true particle in dream UP
entries.русский: мечтать о; (в отрицании) и в мыслях не иметь
entries.separable: no — dream of a house by the water, ✗ dream a house of, ✗ dream it of. Pronouns follow the preposition: I wouldn't dream of it.
entries.verb type: stative — a mental state of longing rather than an act, though it takes the progressive with a temporary reading: she's been dreaming of a year off. The negative wouldn't dream of is a fixed frame.
entries.passive: no — ✗ a year with nothing scheduled is dreamed of by her. Only the attributive participle survives: a long dreamed-of promotion.
entries.see also: dream up, dream on, feel like

entries.meaning: Said to someone whose hopes are unrealistic: not a chance.
examples: A raise this year? Dream on.
Dream on if you think they'll refund the deposit.
"We'll be finished by five." "Dream on."
They can dream on; that parking spot has been spoken for since March.
He asked for a corner office in his first month, and the whole floor told him to dream on.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — dream ON
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate. It is almost always the bare imperative.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in form, but frozen as a bare imperative retort; it has essentially no tensed paradigm beyond they can dream on.
entries.passive: no — the verb takes no object at all, so there is no passive: ✗ it was dreamed on.
entries.see also: dream of, dream up

entries.meaning: To invent something out of nothing, usually something far-fetched.
examples: Who dreamed up this seating chart?
He dreams an excuse up every Monday morning.
Whatever they charge you, they dreamed it up on the spot.
Marketing dreamed up a name nobody can pronounce.
She had dreamed up the whole conspiracy in one sleepless night.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — who dreamed it UP?
entries.separable: yes — dream up an excuse / dream an excuse up, and with a pronoun it must separate: dream it up, never ✗ dream up it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of invention. Progressive is fine — marketing is dreaming up a new name.
entries.passive: yes — the whole seating chart was dreamed up in an afternoon; the conspiracy had been dreamed up in one sleepless night.
entries.see also: dream of, come up with, make up

entries.meaning: To spend or dispel something by drinking — money, an evening, a grief.
examples: He drank away most of the inheritance.
They drank the whole advance away in a month.
She sat at the bar trying to drink the day away.
Whatever he earned, he drank it away by Sunday.
You can't drink away a diagnosis.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, on its second syllable — drink it aWAY
entries.separable: yes — drink away his savings / drink his savings away, and the object-first order is the usual one: drink your troubles away. With a pronoun it must separate: drink it away.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: spending or dispelling money, time, or grief by drinking.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but rare, since the active is what people say: ?most of the inheritance was drunk away inside a year. A diagnosis cannot be: ✗ a diagnosis can't be drunk away is odd outside a joke.
entries.see also: drink up, drink in, eat up

entries.meaning: To take something in with obvious pleasure — a view, applause, a story.
examples: We stood at the rail and drank in the view.
He stood at the podium and drank the applause in.
The crowd went quiet and drank it in.
She drank in every word of the story.
They had drunk in the whole coastline before breakfast.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — drink it IN
entries.separable: yes — drink in the view / drink the view in, and with a pronoun it must separate: drink it in, never ✗ drink in it.
entries.register: everyday — a shade literary, and common in travel writing
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: taking in a view or applause with pleasure. Progressive is normal — they were drinking in the view.
entries.passive: restricted — the passive is stiff and rarely worth using: ?the applause was drunk in. The active carries this verb.
entries.see also: drink up, eat up, drink away

entries.meaning: To raise a glass in honor of someone or something.
examples: Let's drink to the newlyweds.
I'll drink to that.
They drank to absent friends and passed the bottle.
We have drunk to every promotion in this office.
He raised his glass and drank to whoever had paid.
entries.pronunciation note: to is a preposition, so drink keeps the stress
entries.separable: no — drink to your health, ✗ drink your health to, ✗ drink it to. Pronouns follow the preposition: I'll drink to that.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: the single act of raising a glass.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive does not work here: ✗ the newlyweds were drunk to. Only the fixed reply I'll drink to that keeps the object out front, and that is not a passive.
entries.see also: drink up, drink in

entries.meaning: To finish a drink, especially when time is short.
examples: Drink up, the cab's here.
Drink your coffee up before it goes cold.
She poured it out and told him to drink it up.
The kids drank up every drop of the lemonade.
By closing time they had drunk up and gone.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — drink it UP
entries.separable: yes — drink up your milk / drink your milk up, and with a pronoun it must separate: drink it up, never ✗ drink up it. It is just as often used with no object: drink up, we're leaving.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, most often the bare imperative, which takes no object at all: drink up, we're leaving.
entries.passive: restricted — possible with a full object (every drop of the lemonade was drunk up) but rare; the imperative use has nothing to passivize.
entries.see also: drink in, eat up, drink away

entries.meaning: To be hinting at something without saying it outright.
examples: What exactly are you driving at?
I couldn't tell what she was driving at for the first ten minutes.
He kept driving at the same point without ever making it.
If you're driving at something, say it.
Nobody in the room knew what the memo was driving at.
entries.pronunciation note: at is a preposition, so drive keeps the stress
entries.separable: no — what are you driving at, ✗ drive it at. Pronouns follow the preposition.
entries.register: everyday — but nearly always in a question, and nearly always in the progressive
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and effectively locked in the progressive: what are you driving at?, ✗ what do you drive at?
entries.passive: no — ✗ what is being driven at by you? The object stays after the preposition, usually as the question word.
entries.see also: drive home, get at, find out

entries.meaning: To make people leave or stay away, or simply to leave in a vehicle.
examples: The new prices drove half the regulars away.
Rudeness at the front desk drives away more business than bad food.
Say that again and you'll drive them away for good.
The smoke had driven everyone away from the patio.
He got in the truck and drove away without answering.

senses.head: Repel, cause to leave
body: Of customers, friends, or wildlife pushed off by something unpleasant. (отпугивать, отваживать)
examples: The new prices drove half the regulars away.
Rudeness at the front desk drives away more business than bad food.
Say that again and you'll drive them away for good.
The smoke had driven everyone away from the patio.

senses.head: Depart by car
body: The literal sense, with no object. (уехать)
examples: He got in the truck and drove away without answering.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, on its second syllable — drove them aWAY
entries.separable: yes — drive away customers / drive customers away, and with a pronoun it must separate: drive them away, never ✗ drive away them. With no object it simply means leave by car.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: repelling people and simply leaving by car.
entries.passive: yes in the repel sense — half the regulars were driven away by the new prices. No passive of the depart sense, which takes no object.
entries.see also: drive off, drive out, freeze out

entries.meaning: To force a price, a cost, or a rate lower.
examples: Cheap imports drove down the price of steel.
Automation drove labor costs down by a third.
Rates are high, and nothing they've tried drives them down.
The glut has driven wholesale prices down to 2019 levels.
Competition alone won't drive rents down in this city.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — drove them DOWN
entries.separable: yes — drive down costs / drive costs down, and with a pronoun it must separate: drive them down, never ✗ drive down them.
entries.register: everyday — standard in business and news writing
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: forcing a price or a rate lower. Progressive is standard — cheap imports are driving down the price of steel.
entries.passive: yes, and the entry shows it — wholesale prices have been driven down to 2019 levels.
entries.see also: drive up, draw down, drive out

entries.meaning: To make a point land, by repeating it or backing it with evidence.
examples: The photographs drove the point home.
She drove home the cost of doing nothing.
One number drives it home: forty percent never come back.
The coach had driven the lesson home by the third quarter.
Say it again until it's driven home.
entries.pronunciation note: home is an adverb particle here and takes the stress — drove it HOME
entries.separable: yes, and the object-between order is the usual one: drive the point home. Drive home the point is also correct, and with a pronoun it must separate: drive it home, never ✗ drive home it.
entries.register: everyday — plain in argument, coaching, and news writing
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: making a point land by repetition or evidence.
entries.passive: yes, and the entry shows it — say it again until it's driven home; the point was driven home by the photographs.
entries.see also: drive at, get across, drive up

entries.meaning: To force someone or something to retreat, or to leave in a vehicle.
examples: The dogs drove off the coyotes twice that week.
Two guards drove the crowd off the steps.
Whatever it was, the noise drove it off.
She loaded the truck and drove off.
He drove off the first tee and put it in the parking lot.

senses.head: Repel
body: Of an attacker, an animal, or a crowd pushed back. (отбить, прогнать)
examples: The dogs drove off the coyotes twice that week.
Two guards drove the crowd off the steps.
Whatever it was, the noise drove it off.

senses.head: Depart by car
body: No object. (уехать, отъехать)
examples: She loaded the truck and drove off.

senses.head: Hit from the tee
body: Golf. (сделать первый удар с ти)
examples: He drove off the first tee and put it in the parking lot.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — drove them OFF
entries.separable: yes in the repel sense — drive off the raiders / drive the raiders off, and with a pronoun it must separate: drive them off. With no object it means leave by car.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: repelling, leaving by car, and the golf tee shot.
entries.passive: yes in the repel sense — the coyotes were driven off twice that week. No passive of the depart sense, which takes no object.
entries.see also: drive away, drive out, fight off

entries.meaning: To force someone or something to leave a place or a market for good.
examples: The chains drove out every independent bookstore downtown.
Rent increases drove families out of the neighborhood.
Once the big lender moved in, it drove them out in two years.
Bad money drives out good.
The occupying force was finally driven out in the spring.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — drove them OUT
entries.separable: yes — drive out the small operators / drive the small operators out, and with a pronoun it must separate: drive them out, never ✗ drive out them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: forcing someone out of a place or a market.
entries.passive: yes, and the entry shows it — the occupying force was finally driven out in the spring; families were driven out of the neighborhood by rent increases.
entries.see also: drive away, freeze out, drive off

entries.meaning: To push a price, a rate, or a number higher.
examples: The shortage drove up lumber prices all summer.
Every new fee drives the total up.
Demand is what drove them up, not taxes.
Speculation has driven land values up fourfold.
A pickup drove up and two men got out.

senses.head: Push higher
body: Of prices, costs, demand, and premiums. (взвинчивать, поднимать)
examples: The shortage drove up lumber prices all summer.
Every new fee drives the total up.
Demand is what drove them up, not taxes.
Speculation has driven land values up fourfold.

senses.head: Pull up in a vehicle
body: No object. (подъехать)
examples: A pickup drove up and two men got out.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — drove them UP
entries.separable: yes — drive up prices / drive prices up, and with a pronoun it must separate: drive them up, never ✗ drive up them. With no object it means pull up in a vehicle.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: pushing a price or a number higher, or pulling up in a vehicle.
entries.passive: yes in the push-higher sense — land values have been driven up fourfold. No passive of the pull-up sense, which takes no object.
entries.see also: drive down, drive home, draw up

entries.meaning: To wear something down gradually, physically or mentally.
examples: Salt water eats away at the underside of every car here.
Inflation has been eating away at their savings for three years.
The guilt ate away at him until he finally called her.
Small fees eat away at the balance a dollar at a time.
Something's eating away at her and she won't say what.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on away, the particle, not on eat or at
entries.separable: no — ordinary three-part verbs never split. eat away at the foundation, ✗ eat the foundation away at, ✗ eat it away at. Pronouns go at the end: eat away at it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and typically progressive to show the slow wear: inflation has been eating away at their savings.
entries.passive: restricted — the three-part chain passivizes stiffly: ?the foundation has been eaten away at by salt water. Writers drop the at instead: the underside was eaten away.
entries.see also: eat into, eat up, fall apart

entries.meaning: To eat at home rather than at a restaurant.
examples: We're eating in tonight.
They ate in every night that month to save money.
Do you want to eat in or go out?
Since the baby came, they have eaten in almost every night.
It's cheaper to eat in, and it's usually better.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — we're eating IN
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: having the meal at home. Progressive is normal — we're eating in tonight.
entries.passive: no — the verb takes no object at all, so there is no passive: ✗ dinner was eaten in.
entries.see also: eat out, eat up

entries.meaning: To use up part of something you were trying to preserve — money, time, or a margin.
examples: The repairs ate into our vacation fund.
Two hours of meetings eat into every workday.
Returns are eating into the margin.
The delay had eaten into the schedule badly.
Interest eats into whatever you manage to save.
entries.pronunciation note: into is a preposition, so eat keeps the stress; compare the true particle in eat UP
entries.separable: no — eat into the profits, ✗ eat the profits into, ✗ eat it into. Pronouns follow the preposition: eat into it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: consuming part of a fund, a margin, or a schedule. Progressive is common — returns are eating into the margin.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is marginal at best: ?the vacation fund was eaten into by the repairs. The active is what gets written.
entries.see also: eat away at, eat up, dig into

entries.meaning: To have a meal at a restaurant rather than at home.
examples: We eat out maybe twice a month.
They ate out every night of the trip.
He hasn't eaten out since the diagnosis.
Nobody eats out on a Tuesday in this town.
If you eat out that often, the budget's gone by the fifteenth.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — we ate OUT
entries.русский: есть вне дома, ходить в ресторан
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: taking the meal at a restaurant.
entries.passive: no — the verb takes no object at all: ✗ dinner was eaten out. (He hasn't eaten out since the diagnosis is a perfect, not a passive.)
entries.see also: eat in, eat up

entries.meaning: To finish food, to consume time or money, or to lap something up eagerly.
examples: Eat up — we're leaving in ten minutes.
The kids ate the whole pan up before dinner.
The commute eats up two hours a day.
Legal fees ate the settlement up.
He told the story again and the crowd ate it up.
She's eaten up with jealousy and everyone can see it.

senses.head: Finish food
body: Often an imperative aimed at children. (съесть без остатка, доесть)
examples: Eat up — we're leaving in ten minutes.
The kids ate the whole pan up before dinner.

senses.head: Consume time or money
body: Of a commute, a legal bill, a project — anything that swallows a resource. (поглощать, съедать)
examples: The commute eats up two hours a day.
Legal fees ate the settlement up.

senses.head: Lap up, believe eagerly
body: Of an audience delighted by something, or of someone swallowing a story whole. (проглотить, охотно поверить)
examples: He told the story again and the crowd ate it up.

senses.head: Be eaten up with
body: Consumed by an emotion — jealousy, guilt, worry. Passive only. (снедаемый, изводимый)
examples: She's eaten up with jealousy and everyone can see it.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — ate it UP
entries.русский: съесть без остатка; поглощать (время, деньги); проглотить, охотно поверить
entries.separable: yes — eat up the leftovers / eat the leftovers up, and with a pronoun it must separate: eat it up, never ✗ eat up it. As a bare imperative it takes no object: eat up!
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: finishing food, consuming a resource, lapping something up, and the passive-only be eaten up with.
entries.passive: yes — the settlement was eaten up by legal fees; the whole pan was eaten up before dinner. Sense 4 exists only as a passive: she's eaten up with jealousy.
entries.see also: eat into, drink up, eat away at

entries.meaning: To break into pieces, to collapse as an arrangement, or to lose emotional control.
examples: The binder fell apart the first week.
The porch steps had fallen apart long before they bought the place.
The deal fell apart over one clause.
Their marriage has been falling apart for years.
Everything falls apart if the delivery is late.
She kept it together at the funeral and fell apart in the car.

senses.head: Come to pieces
body: Of cheap objects and old buildings. (разваливаться на части)
examples: The binder fell apart the first week.
The porch steps had fallen apart long before they bought the place.

senses.head: Collapse as an arrangement
body: Of deals, plans, marriages, and coalitions. (разваливаться, рушиться)
examples: The deal fell apart over one clause.
Their marriage has been falling apart for years.
Everything falls apart if the delivery is late.

senses.head: Break down emotionally
body: Of a person who can no longer hold it together. (сломаться, расклеиться)
examples: She kept it together at the funeral and fell apart in the car.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle apart, on its second syllable
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a process verb; the progressive is natural for the slow senses (their marriage has been falling apart for years).
entries.passive: no — intransitive in all three senses, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the binder was fallen apart, ✗ the deal was fallen apart over one clause.
entries.see also: fall through, fall down, break down

entries.meaning: To retreat, or to move back to a safer or lower position.
examples: The line fell back to the second ridge.
The crowd fell back to let the stretcher through.
Sales fell back after the holidays.
He had fallen back to third place by the last lap.
Rather than argue, he fell back a step and let her finish.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fell BACK
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate. Do not confuse it with fall back on, which is a different, three-part verb.
entries.register: everyday — the retreat sense is military in origin and now ordinary in business writing too
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a movement verb: literal with troops and crowds, figurative with numbers (sales fell back after the holidays).
entries.passive: no — no object at all: ✗ the second ridge was fallen back to. Only the separate verb fall back on takes anything.
entries.see also: fall back on, draw back, fall behind

entries.meaning: To resort to something dependable when the first option fails.
examples: If the grant doesn't come through, we can fall back on the endowment.
He fell back on the same three jokes all night.
She has a teaching license to fall back on.
When the numbers ran out, the report fell back on anecdotes.
There's nothing to fall back on if this one fails.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle back, not on fall and not on on
entries.русский: прибегать к, опираться на (в крайнем случае)
entries.separable: no — ordinary three-part verbs never split. fall back on savings, ✗ fall savings back on, ✗ fall it back on. Pronouns go at the end: fall back on it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the act of resorting to something when the first option fails (the report fell back on anecdotes), not a state.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is grammatical but strained: ?the same three jokes were fallen back on all night. Americans recast with resort to or rely on.
entries.see also: fall back, draw on, get by

entries.meaning: To end up further back than the others, or to get late with payments or work.
examples: He fell behind the rest of the class in two months.
Production has fallen behind schedule again.
Miss two weeks and you fall behind for the whole semester.
She never falls behind, even with three projects going.
They fell behind on the mortgage after the layoff.

senses.head: Lag behind
body: Of a runner, a student, a schedule. (отставать)
examples: He fell behind the rest of the class in two months.
Production has fallen behind schedule again.
Miss two weeks and you fall behind for the whole semester.
She never falls behind, even with three projects going.

senses.head: Get in arrears
body: Of payments, with on. (просрочить платежи, залезть в долги)
examples: They fell behind on the mortgage after the layoff.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the second syllable of behind; fall is unstressed
entries.separable: no — fall behind the others, ✗ fall the others behind, ✗ fall it behind. It is just as often used with no object at all: don't fall behind.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a gradual process, comfortable in the progressive (production has been falling behind all quarter).
entries.passive: no — behind stays a preposition of position and will not promote: ✗ the rest of the class was fallen behind by him, ✗ the mortgage was fallen behind on.
entries.see also: fall back, catch up, keep up

entries.meaning: To drop to the ground, or — of an argument, plan, or system — to fail at a particular point.
examples: The whole fence fell down in the storm.
He fell down the last three steps.
That's exactly where the argument falls down.
The plan falls down on cost.
They have fallen down badly on follow-up.

senses.head: Drop to the ground
body: The literal sense, of people and structures. (упасть, обвалиться)
examples: The whole fence fell down in the storm.
He fell down the last three steps.

senses.head: Fail, prove inadequate
body: Of a theory or a service, usually with on: the place where it stops working. (хромать, не выдерживать критики)
examples: That's exactly where the argument falls down.
The plan falls down on cost.
They have fallen down badly on follow-up.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fell DOWN
entries.русский: упасть; не выдерживать критики, хромать (об аргументе)
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate. When a place follows, down is a preposition and stays put: fell down the stairs, ✗ fell the stairs down.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a body or a structure dropping in sense 1, an argument that stops working in sense 2 (the plan falls down on cost).
entries.passive: no — intransitive: ✗ the last three steps were fallen down, ✗ follow-up has been fallen down on.
entries.see also: fall apart, fall through, fall off

entries.meaning: To be taken in by a trick, or to fall in love with someone.
examples: Thousands of people fell for the same email.
I can't believe you fell for it.
Don't fall for the free-trial pitch.
He fell for her the first week of the job.
She'd fallen for the city before the week was out.

senses.head: Be deceived by
body: Of a scam, a line, a pitch. (повестись на, попасться на)
examples: Thousands of people fell for the same email.
I can't believe you fell for it.
Don't fall for the free-trial pitch.

senses.head: Fall in love with
body: Of a person, and by extension of a city or a house. (влюбиться в)
examples: He fell for her the first week of the job.
She'd fallen for the city before the week was out.

entries.pronunciation note: for is a preposition, so fall keeps the stress
entries.русский: повестись на, попасться на; влюбиться в
entries.separable: no — fall for the scam, ✗ fall the scam for, ✗ fall it for. Pronouns follow the preposition: she fell for it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; each names an event, not a state — he fell for her the first week of the job.
entries.passive: no — ✗ the same email was fallen for by thousands, ✗ she was fallen for. Use be taken in by for the trick sense.
entries.see also: fall in with, find out, take in

entries.meaning: To collapse inward, or to get into formation.
examples: The roof fell in under the weight of the snow.
Part of the tunnel had fallen in years before.
If the bank of sand falls in, the trench goes with it.
The whole platoon fell in before dawn.
Fall in — two ranks, on the road.

senses.head: Cave in
body: Of roofs, trenches, and tunnels. (обвалиться, провалиться)
examples: The roof fell in under the weight of the snow.
Part of the tunnel had fallen in years before.
If the bank of sand falls in, the trench goes with it.

senses.head: Get into formation
body: Military, usually an order. The opposite command is fall out. (строиться, встать в строй)
examples: The whole platoon fell in before dawn.
Fall in — two ranks, on the road.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fell IN
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate.
entries.register: everyday — the line-up sense is military
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a collapse in sense 1, a maneuver in sense 2, where it is usually an order (Fall in — two ranks, on the road).
entries.passive: no — neither sense takes an object: ✗ the tunnel was fallen in, ✗ the platoon was fallen in before dawn.
entries.see also: fall down, fall in with, fall out

entries.meaning: To start running with a group, usually a bad one, or to go along with a plan.
examples: He fell in with a bad crowd his first year away from home.
She fell in with a group of climbers in Denver and never came home.
The others fell in with the plan without much argument.
Two of the board members have fallen in with the buyer's position.
It's easy to fall in with whatever the room already believes.

senses.head: Take up with people
body: Almost always with a crowd the speaker disapproves of. (связаться с, спутаться с)
examples: He fell in with a bad crowd his first year away from home.
She fell in with a group of climbers in Denver and never came home.

senses.head: Go along with a plan
body: To agree to someone else's proposal without much resistance. (согласиться с, поддержать)
examples: The others fell in with the plan without much argument.
Two of the board members have fallen in with the buyer's position.
It's easy to fall in with whatever the room already believes.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle in, not on fall and not on with
entries.separable: no — ordinary three-part verbs never split. fall in with a bad crowd, ✗ fall a bad crowd in with, ✗ fall it in with. Pronouns go at the end: fall in with them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; both senses name something that happens at a point in time — meeting a crowd, or coming around to a plan.
entries.passive: no — ✗ a bad crowd was fallen in with, ✗ the plan was fallen in with without much argument. Recast as took up with or went along with.
entries.see also: fall for, fit in with, fall out

entries.meaning: To decrease, or to come loose and drop.
examples: Attendance fell off sharply after the first month.
Quality has fallen off since the plant moved.
Orders fell off a cliff in March.
The handle fell off the second time I used it.
He fell off the ladder and broke his wrist.

senses.head: Decline in number or quality
body: Of attendance, sales, orders, and standards. (снижаться, падать)
examples: Attendance fell off sharply after the first month.
Quality has fallen off since the plant moved.
Orders fell off a cliff in March.

senses.head: Come loose and drop
body: Literal, of parts and of people. (отвалиться; свалиться)
examples: The handle fell off the second time I used it.
He fell off the ladder and broke his wrist.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fell OFF
entries.separable: there is no object in the decline sense, so there is nothing to separate. When a place follows, off is a preposition and stays put: fall off the ladder, ✗ fall the ladder off.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a gradual decline in sense 1 (quality has been falling off), a single event in sense 2 (the handle fell off).
entries.passive: no — intransitive; what follows the literal fall off belongs to the preposition: ✗ the ladder was fallen off.
entries.see also: fall behind, fall apart, drive down

entries.meaning: For a date to land on a given day, for a duty to land on a person, or to attack.
examples: Christmas falls on a Tuesday this year.
The cost falls on the tenant, not the landlord.
It fell on her to tell the family.
They fell on the food like they hadn't eaten in days.
The mill closed and the town fell on hard times.

senses.head: Land on, of a date
body: Of holidays and anniversaries. (выпадать на, приходиться на)
examples: Christmas falls on a Tuesday this year.

senses.head: Become someone's responsibility
body: Of a cost or a duty nobody volunteered for. (ложиться на, выпадать на долю)
examples: The cost falls on the tenant, not the landlord.
It fell on her to tell the family.

senses.head: Attack, set upon
body: Of people or animals rushing at something. Slightly literary. (наброситься на)
examples: They fell on the food like they hadn't eaten in days.

senses.head: Fall on hard times
body: A fixed phrase for coming into poverty or decline. (обеднеть, знать лучшие времена)
examples: The mill closed and the town fell on hard times.

entries.pronunciation note: on is a preposition here, so fall keeps the stress; compare the true particle in fall OFF
entries.русский: выпадать на (о дате); ложиться на (об обязанности); наброситься на
entries.separable: no — fall on a Sunday, ✗ fall a Sunday on, ✗ fall it on. Pronouns follow the preposition: it fell on her.
entries.register: everyday — the attack sense is a shade literary
entries.verb type: stative in the date and duty senses — a standing fact, ✗ Christmas is falling on a Tuesday; action (dynamic) in the attack sense, they fell on the food.
entries.passive: restricted — only the attack sense, and it reads literary: the wagons were fallen on before dawn. ✗ a Tuesday is fallen on by Christmas, ✗ the tenant is fallen on by the cost.
entries.see also: fall under, fall out, fall through

entries.meaning: To quarrel and stop speaking, for something attached to come loose, or to leave military formation.
examples: The two brothers fell out over the will.
She fell out with her business partner and sold her half.
His hair started falling out during treatment.
The screws had fallen out one by one.
The company fell out and headed for the mess hall.

senses.head: Quarrel
body: Usually fall out with someone, over something. Americans more often say have a falling-out. (поссориться, разругаться)
examples: The two brothers fell out over the will.
She fell out with her business partner and sold her half.

senses.head: Come loose and drop
body: Of hair, teeth, screws. (выпадать, вываливаться)
examples: His hair started falling out during treatment.
The screws had fallen out one by one.

senses.head: Leave formation
body: Military, the opposite of fall in. (выйти из строя, разойтись)
examples: The company fell out and headed for the mess hall.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fell OUT
entries.русский: поссориться; выпадать (о волосах, зубах); выйти из строя
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate. The person you quarrel with follows with: fell out with her partner, ✗ fell her partner out with.
entries.register: everyday — in American English the quarrel sense is usually the noun, a falling-out; the verb fall out with is more British
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: quarreling, hair or screws coming loose, a company leaving formation.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; the person you quarrel with is the object of with, not of the verb: ✗ her business partner was fallen out with.
entries.see also: fall in, fall in with, fall through

entries.meaning: For an arrangement to collapse before it can happen.
examples: The sale fell through two days before closing.
Their financing fell through and the whole project stopped.
If this falls through, we're out the deposit.
Three offers had fallen through by August.
Plans fall through around here constantly.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fell THROUGH
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; an event, the collapse of an arrangement before it can happen (the sale fell through two days before closing).
entries.passive: no — intransitive, no object: ✗ the sale was fallen through, ✗ the financing was fallen through.
entries.see also: fall apart, fall down, come through

entries.meaning: To belong in a category, or to come within someone's authority.
examples: Anything under fifty dollars falls under petty cash.
The site falls under federal jurisdiction, not the county's.
Two of the charges fell under the older statute.
Those complaints fall under HR.
The whole department fell under her control after the merger.

senses.head: Be classified as
body: Of items assigned to a heading, a budget line, or a statute. (подпадать под, относиться к)
examples: Anything under fifty dollars falls under petty cash.
The site falls under federal jurisdiction, not the county's.
Two of the charges fell under the older statute.

senses.head: Come under someone's control
body: Of a department, or of a person under an influence — fall under the spell of. (перейти в ведение; попасть под влияние)
examples: Those complaints fall under HR.
The whole department fell under her control after the merger.

entries.pronunciation note: under is a preposition, so fall keeps the stress
entries.separable: no — fall under state law, ✗ fall state law under, ✗ fall it under. Pronouns follow the preposition: those fall under it.
entries.register: formal — legal, administrative, and classifying language
entries.verb type: stative in the classifying sense — a standing fact, ✗ the site is falling under federal jurisdiction; dynamic when it names a change of hands (the department fell under her control after the merger).
entries.passive: no — ✗ petty cash is fallen under by anything under fifty dollars, ✗ HR is fallen under by those complaints. Say is covered by or comes under.
entries.see also: fall on, fit in with, deal with

entries.meaning: To return information to the place it came from.
examples: The sensors feed back temperature readings every second.
Please feed the survey results back to the team by Friday.
Whatever the testers find, feed it back to engineering.
The output is fed back into the input, which is where the noun comes from.
She fed back two pages of notes on the draft.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — feed it BACK; the noun feedback moves the stress to the front, FEED-back
entries.separable: yes — feed back the results / feed the results back, and with a pronoun it must separate: feed them back, never ✗ feed back them.
entries.register: everyday — workplace and engineering talk; the noun feedback is far more common than the verb
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a transfer of information, mechanical (the sensors feed back readings every second) or human (she fed back two pages of notes).
entries.passive: yes — the output is fed back into the input, which is where the noun feedback comes from; the survey results were fed back to the team on Friday.
entries.see also: feed into, feed off, find out

entries.meaning: To contribute to something larger, or to flow into it.
examples: Every one of those complaints feeds into the same problem.
The creek feeds into the reservoir north of town.
Coverage like that feeds into the panic.
Their data feeds into the national model.
His resentment had been feeding into every meeting for a year.
entries.pronunciation note: into is a preposition, so feed keeps the stress; compare the true particle in feed BACK
entries.русский: питать, подпитывать; вливаться в, влиять на
entries.separable: no — feed into the debate, ✗ feed the debate into, ✗ feed it into. (The literal feed the paper into the printer is a different pattern, with a direct object before into.)
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a continuing contribution, at home in the progressive (his resentment had been feeding into every meeting for a year).
entries.passive: no — ✗ the same problem is fed into by every complaint, ✗ the panic is fed into by coverage like that. (The literal the paper is fed into the printer is a different pattern, with a direct object.)
entries.see also: feed off, feed back, eat into

entries.meaning: To take sustenance or energy from something, literally or figuratively.
examples: The birds feed off whatever the tide leaves.
He feeds off an audience — the bigger the better.
The two rumors fed off each other all week.
That industry feeds off people's fear of missing out.
She's been feeding off other people's work for years.

senses.head: Take food from
body: Of animals and of what a place leaves behind. (питаться чем-либо, кормиться)
examples: The birds feed off whatever the tide leaves.

senses.head: Draw energy or advantage from
body: Of performers and crowds, of rumors that reinforce each other, of industries that profit from a weakness. (подпитываться, кормиться за счёт)
examples: He feeds off an audience — the bigger the better.
The two rumors fed off each other all week.
That industry feeds off people's fear of missing out.
She's been feeding off other people's work for years.

entries.pronunciation note: off is a preposition here, so feed keeps the stress
entries.separable: no — feed off the crowd, ✗ feed the crowd off, ✗ feed it off. Pronouns follow the preposition: they feed off it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; taking food or energy over time, and the progressive is normal (she's been feeding off other people's work for years).
entries.passive: no — ✗ the crowd is fed off by him, ✗ people's fear of missing out is fed off. Recast active, or use live off of.
entries.see also: feed on, feed into, eat away at

entries.meaning: For an animal to eat a particular food, or for a feeling to be sustained by something.
examples: Bats feed on insects, not fruit, in this part of the country.
The larvae feed on the bark all summer.
Suspicion feeds on silence.
The campaign fed on every retraction the paper printed.
Panic had fed on rumor for a week before anyone checked.

senses.head: Eat habitually
body: The standard verb in natural history writing. (питаться чем-либо)
examples: Bats feed on insects, not fruit, in this part of the country.
The larvae feed on the bark all summer.

senses.head: Be sustained by
body: Of fear, suspicion, rumor, resentment. (подпитываться, питаться)
examples: Suspicion feeds on silence.
The campaign fed on every retraction the paper printed.
Panic had fed on rumor for a week before anyone checked.

entries.pronunciation note: on is a preposition, so feed keeps the stress
entries.separable: no — feed on insects, ✗ feed insects on, ✗ feed it on. (The look-alike feed the dog on scraps is a different pattern, with a direct object before on.)
entries.register: everyday — the biological sense is the standard one in natural history writing; the figurative sense is a shade literary
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; habitual eating in sense 1, a continuing process in sense 2 (panic had fed on rumor for a week).
entries.passive: no — ✗ insects are fed on by bats, ✗ silence is fed on by suspicion. The natural the dog was fed on scraps belongs to the other pattern, where the dog is the direct object.
entries.see also: feed off, feed into

entries.meaning: To fatten someone up with food; in the fixed form fed up, to have had more than enough of something.
examples: His grandmother spent the whole summer feeding him up.
Two weeks of home cooking fed the boy up nicely.
They sent her to the coast to be fed up after the illness.
I'm fed up with the excuses.
She got fed up and quit in October.
Everyone on that floor is fed up with the noise.

senses.head: Fatten someone up
body: British, said of someone thin after an illness or a hard stretch. (откармливать, отпаивать)
examples: His grandmother spent the whole summer feeding him up.
Two weeks of home cooking fed the boy up nicely.
They sent her to the coast to be fed up after the illness.

senses.head: Be fed up with
body: The everyday American form: sick of something, out of patience. Always passive, and the thing you are sick of follows with. (быть сытым по горло, надоесть)
examples: I'm fed up with the excuses.
She got fed up and quit in October.
Everyone on that floor is fed up with the noise.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fed him UP; in the fixed adjective fed up the stress sits on up too
entries.русский: откармливать; (be fed up) быть сытым по горло
entries.separable: yes in the fatten sense — feed up the boy / feed the boy up, and with a pronoun it must separate: feed him up, never ✗ feed up him. The far more common American form is the fixed participle fed up, which takes no object at all.
entries.transitive: yes in the active sense; the common be fed up (with) form is passive
entries.register: everyday — fed up with is everyday American; the active feed someone up, meaning fatten, is British
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the fatten sense; the fixed be fed up (with) is stative — a state of exasperation, ✗ I am being fed up with the excuses.
entries.passive: yes — they sent her to the coast to be fed up after the illness, and the everyday American form exists only in passive shape: I'm fed up with the excuses, she got fed up and quit.
entries.see also: eat up, feed off, put up with

entries.meaning: To feel sympathy for someone, or to grope for something you cannot see.
examples: I really feel for her — that's a terrible position to be in.
You have to feel for anyone who gets that news by email.
Nobody felt for the manager after what he said.
He felt for the light switch in the dark.
She was feeling for the edge of the step with her cane.

senses.head: Sympathize with
body: A short way of saying you understand how bad someone's position is. (сочувствовать, жалеть)
examples: I really feel for her — that's a terrible position to be in.
You have to feel for anyone who gets that news by email.
Nobody felt for the manager after what he said.

senses.head: Grope for
body: Literal: searching with your hands in the dark or out of sight. (нащупывать)
examples: He felt for the light switch in the dark.
She was feeling for the edge of the step with her cane.

entries.pronunciation note: for is a preposition, so feel keeps the stress
entries.separable: no — feel for her, ✗ feel her for. Pronouns follow the preposition: I feel for them.
