entries.verb type: stative in the sympathy sense — a feeling, not an act (I really feel for her); action (dynamic) in the grope sense, where the progressive is normal: she was feeling for the edge of the step.
entries.passive: no — ✗ she was felt for by everyone, ✗ the light switch was felt for in the dark. Do not confuse it with feel up, which passivizes freely.
entries.see also: feel up to, feel like, fall for

entries.meaning: To want something, or to seem a certain way to the senses.
examples: I feel like a nap.
Nobody felt like cooking, so we ordered.
Do you feel like driving, or should I?
It feels like November out there.
That meeting felt like three hours.

senses.head: Want, be in the mood for
body: Followed by a noun or an -ing form, never by a to-infinitive: ✗ feel like to go. (хотеть, быть в настроении)
examples: I feel like a nap.
Nobody felt like cooking, so we ordered.
Do you feel like driving, or should I?

senses.head: Seem, give the impression of
body: Of weather, of a room, of how long something took. (ощущаться как, казаться)
examples: It feels like November out there.
That meeting felt like three hours.

entries.pronunciation note: like is a preposition, so feel keeps the stress
entries.русский: хотеть, быть в настроении; ощущаться как
entries.separable: no — feel like a nap, ✗ feel a nap like, ✗ feel it like. Pronouns follow the preposition: I don't feel like it.
entries.verb type: stative in both senses — a mood in sense 1 (✗ I am feeling like a nap) and a perception in sense 2, where feel is linking: it feels like November out there.
entries.passive: no — stative perception, and like is a preposition rather than an object marker: ✗ a nap is felt like, ✗ three hours was felt like by that meeting.
entries.see also: feel up to, feel for, do with

entries.meaning: To probe someone's position carefully before committing to anything.
examples: Feel out the board before you put anything in writing.
He felt two of the partners out over lunch.
Call her and feel her out on the timing.
They're feeling the market out with a small run.
Nobody had felt him out about the job before the offer went in.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — feel them OUT
entries.separable: yes — feel out the board / feel the board out, and with a pronoun it must separate: feel them out, never ✗ feel out them.
entries.register: informal — chiefly American; British speakers say sound out
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; deliberate probing, fine in the progressive (they're feeling the market out with a small run).
entries.passive: yes — he hadn't been felt out about the job before the offer went in; two of the partners were felt out over lunch.
entries.see also: find out, feel up to, dig into

entries.meaning: To touch someone sexually, usually without invitation.
examples: He got thrown out of the bar for feeling a customer up.
She reported that a man on the train had felt her up.
Nobody should have to worry about being felt up on the way to work.
Two complaints said the same manager had felt people up at the party.
If he feels anyone up again, he's fired.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — felt her UP
entries.separable: yes, and with a pronoun it must separate: feel her up, never ✗ feel up her. With a full noun both orders occur, but the object-between order is the usual one.
entries.register: vulgar — crude, and out of place in polite or professional talk; note that feel up to is a completely unrelated verb
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a physical act, and it takes the progressive: he was feeling her up on the train.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is how the complaint is usually worded — nobody should have to worry about being felt up on the way to work.
entries.see also: feel up to, feel out

entries.meaning: To feel well enough or strong enough for something.
examples: I don't feel up to a three-hour drive today.
She didn't feel up to explaining it again.
If you feel up to it, come by around six.
He hasn't felt up to much since the surgery.
Nobody felt up to another round of interviews.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle up, not on feel and not on to
entries.русский: чувствовать в себе силы, быть в состоянии
entries.separable: no — ordinary three-part verbs never split. feel up to a long drive, ✗ feel a long drive up to, ✗ feel it up to. Pronouns go at the end: I don't feel up to it.
entries.verb type: stative — a state of readiness rather than an act (he hasn't felt up to much since the surgery); the progressive shows up only in the softened I'm not feeling up to it today.
entries.passive: no — ✗ a three-hour drive isn't felt up to, ✗ another round of interviews wasn't felt up to by anyone. The complement stays after to.
entries.see also: feel like, feel for, fit in

entries.meaning: To resist an attack instead of taking it, or to hold an emotion in.
examples: She fought back and the whole thing ended up in court.
The union fought back with a work stoppage.
He fought back tears through the whole eulogy.
She fought a smile back and kept reading.
Whatever he was feeling, he fought it back.

senses.head: Resist, retaliate
body: No object. Of a person, a union, a campaign. (давать отпор, сопротивляться)
examples: She fought back and the whole thing ended up in court.
The union fought back with a work stoppage.

senses.head: Suppress an emotion
body: The object is tears, a smile, panic, nausea — something rising that you push down. (сдерживать, подавлять)
examples: He fought back tears through the whole eulogy.
She fought a smile back and kept reading.
Whatever he was feeling, he fought it back.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fought BACK
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — fight back the tears / fight the tears back, and with a pronoun it must separate: fight them back. In the resist sense there is no object at all: she fought back.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: retaliating in sense 1, pushing an emotion down in sense 2 (he fought back tears through the whole eulogy).
entries.passive: restricted — only sense 2, and it reads bookish: the tears were fought back until the car door closed. Sense 1 takes no object at all: ✗ it was fought back by the union.
entries.see also: fight off, fight down, fight out

entries.meaning: To suppress a feeling that is trying to surface.
examples: He fought down the urge to answer.
She fought her panic down and finished the presentation.
Whatever the impulse was, he fought it down.
The witness fought down his anger long enough to testify.
She'd fought the same nausea down every morning that week.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fought it DOWN
entries.separable: yes — fight down the urge / fight the urge down, and with a pronoun it must separate: fight it down, never ✗ fight down it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the deliberate suppression of a feeling as it rises, commonest in narrative past (she fought her panic down and finished the presentation).
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical, with the feeling as subject — the urge was fought down and nothing was said — but rare; American writing keeps this one active.
entries.see also: fight back, fight off, hold back

entries.meaning: To repel an attacker, or to hold off an illness, sleep, or a rival.
examples: She fought off the dog with a backpack.
They had fought the raiders off twice before.
He's been fighting a cold off all week.
I had three cups of coffee and still couldn't fight it off.
The incumbent fought off two primary challengers.

senses.head: Repel an attack
body: Of a person, an animal, or an armed force pushed back. (отбиваться от, отбить)
examples: She fought off the dog with a backpack.
They had fought the raiders off twice before.

senses.head: Resist an illness or a state
body: Of a cold, the flu, sleep — something coming over you. (побороть, перебороть)
examples: He's been fighting a cold off all week.
I had three cups of coffee and still couldn't fight it off.

senses.head: Hold off competitors
body: Of a challenger, a bid, a takeover. (отбить, отразить)
examples: The incumbent fought off two primary challengers.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fought it OFF
entries.separable: yes — fight off a cold / fight a cold off, and with a pronoun it must separate: fight it off, never ✗ fight off it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: repelling an attacker, holding off an illness, beating back a rival.
entries.passive: yes — the raiders had been fought off twice before; two primary challengers were fought off; a cold that can't be fought off with coffee.
entries.see also: fight back, drive off, fight down

entries.meaning: To settle a dispute by fighting or arguing it through to a finish.
examples: Let them fight it out and stay out of it.
The two departments fought it out over three budget cycles.
They fought the last two seats out in court.
We'll fight it out in the morning.
The candidates had fought it out to a tie.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fight it OUT
entries.русский: выяснить отношения, решить спор до конца
entries.separable: yes, and in practice it is always separated, because the object is nearly always it: fight it out, never ✗ fight out it. With a full noun the object also usually comes first: fought the last two seats out in court.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; settling a dispute by carrying it through to a finish, usually with the near-empty object it (let them fight it out).
entries.passive: restricted — fine with a real object, the last two seats were fought out in court, but the ordinary fight it out has no passive: ✗ it was fought out by the two departments.
entries.see also: fight back, fight off, deal with

entries.meaning: For a court, jury, or panel to decide a case in someone's favor.
examples: The jury found for the plaintiff on all four counts.
The court found for the defendant and dismissed the case.
If the panel finds for the company, the fee stands.
The judge found against the city on the permit question.
Two of the three arbitrators had found for the union.
entries.pronunciation note: for is a preposition, so find keeps the stress; compare the true particle in find OUT
entries.separable: no — find for the plaintiff, ✗ find the plaintiff for, ✗ find it for. The opposite, find against, behaves exactly the same way.
entries.register: formal — courtroom language; outside a legal setting people say rule in favor of
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a courtroom act, the moment a verdict is returned (the jury found for the plaintiff on all four counts).
entries.passive: no — ✗ the plaintiff was found for, ✗ the city was found against. Court reporting says judgment was entered for the plaintiff instead.
entries.see also: find out, fall under, deal with

entries.meaning: To learn a fact, or to expose someone who has been hiding something.
examples: Call the office and find out what time it closes.
I found out about the layoffs from a group chat.
She found the address out in about ten seconds.
We'll find out on Thursday.
Sooner or later they'll find him out.
Nobody knew, and nobody ever found her out.

senses.head: Learn, discover
body: The ordinary sense, most often with a clause or with about. (выяснить, узнать)
examples: Call the office and find out what time it closes.
I found out about the layoffs from a group chat.
She found the address out in about ten seconds.
We'll find out on Thursday.

senses.head: Expose someone
body: Of a person whose deception finally shows. Object always between the two words. (раскусить, вывести на чистую воду)
examples: Sooner or later they'll find him out.
Nobody knew, and nobody ever found her out.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — found it OUT
entries.separable: yes — find out the answer / find the answer out, and with a pronoun it must separate: find it out, never ✗ find out it. When the object is a clause the phrase stays whole: find out what happened, ✗ find what happened out. Of a person, the separated order is the idiom: they found him out.
entries.transitive: either — it also stands alone: we'll find out
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the event of knowledge arriving (we'll find out on Thursday), not a state like know.
entries.passive: yes — strongest in the expose sense: sooner or later he'll be found out, nobody knew, and she was never found out. Also the layoffs were found out about within a day.
entries.see also: dig up, feel out, find for

entries.meaning: To belong comfortably in a group, or to find room or time for something.
examples: He never really fit in at that school.
It took her a year to fit in on the crew.
Can the doctor fit me in on Thursday?
She fit two more errands in before noon.
We can fit it in after lunch if you're quick.

senses.head: Belong socially
body: No object. Note that in American English the past is fit, not fitted: he never fit in. (вписываться, приживаться)
examples: He never really fit in at that school.
It took her a year to fit in on the crew.

senses.head: Squeeze into a schedule or a space
body: Of appointments, errands, and one more chair. (втиснуть, вместить)
examples: Can the doctor fit me in on Thursday?
She fit two more errands in before noon.
We can fit it in after lunch if you're quick.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fit me IN
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — fit in an appointment / fit an appointment in, and with a pronoun it must separate: can you fit me in?, never ✗ fit in me. In the belong sense there is no object: she never fit in.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the scheduling sense (she fit two more errands in before noon); closer to stative in the belong sense, a standing fact about a person: he never really fit in at that school.
entries.passive: restricted — only the scheduling sense, and it is ordinary office talk: I was fit in between two other appointments. The belong sense has no object: ✗ that school was never fit in.
entries.see also: fit in with, fit out, feel out

entries.meaning: To be compatible with a plan, a schedule, a style, or a group.
examples: Does Tuesday fit in with your schedule?
The addition doesn't fit in with the rest of the block.
Her findings don't fit in with the model at all.
He never fit in with the people his brother ran around with.
We'll do whatever fits in with the delivery window.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the particle in, not on fit and not on with
entries.separable: no — ordinary three-part verbs never split. fit in with the plan, ✗ fit the plan in with, ✗ fit it in with. Pronouns go at the end: fit in with it.
entries.verb type: stative — compatibility, a standing relation rather than an act; the progressive is odd: ✗ Tuesday is fitting in with your schedule.
entries.passive: no — one of the fit / suit / match group that refuses the passive even with something after it: ✗ your schedule is fit in with by Tuesday, ✗ the model isn't fit in with by her findings.
entries.see also: fit in, fall in with, fall under

entries.meaning: To supply a place, a vehicle, or a person with the equipment needed.
examples: They fit out the whole clinic for under a hundred thousand.
He fit the van out with bunks and a sink.
The store came empty and we fit it out ourselves.
The schooner was fitted out for a two-year voyage.
Every truck gets fitted out with a second radio.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fit it OUT
entries.separable: yes — fit out the clinic / fit the clinic out, and with a pronoun it must separate: fit it out, never ✗ fit out it.
entries.register: everyday — boats, shops, and crews; British speakers also say fit up in this sense
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the work of equipping a place, a vehicle, or a crew (they fit out the whole clinic for under a hundred thousand).
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is at least as common as the active — the schooner was fitted out for a two-year voyage, every truck gets fitted out with a second radio.
entries.see also: fit up, do up, draw up

entries.meaning: To frame someone for a crime they did not commit, or to equip a place.
examples: He always claimed the squad fitted him up.
Two detectives were accused of fitting up a witness.
If they want you, they'll fit you up.
They fitted the flat up as an office.
The gym was fitted up with donated equipment.

senses.head: Frame someone
body: British criminal slang, and the usual word in British police dramas. (подставить, сфабриковать дело)
examples: He always claimed the squad fitted him up.
Two detectives were accused of fitting up a witness.
If they want you, they'll fit you up.

senses.head: Equip, kit out
body: British, the same sense as American fit out. (оборудовать, обставить)
examples: They fitted the flat up as an office.
The gym was fitted up with donated equipment.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — fitted him UP
entries.separable: yes — fit up the flat / fit the flat up, and with a pronoun it must separate: they fitted him up, never ✗ they fitted up him.
entries.register: British — informal, police and crime slang; Americans say frame or set up
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: framing someone in sense 1, equipping a place in sense 2.
entries.passive: yes — he always claimed he'd been fitted up by the squad; the gym was fitted up with donated equipment.
entries.see also: fit out, do over, set up

entries.meaning: To attack someone suddenly, with fists or with words.
examples: She flew at him before anyone could stand up.
The dog flew at the mailman through the screen door.
He flew at the referee over a call in the first period.
Two of them had flown at each other by the second round.
Say the wrong thing and she'll fly at you.
entries.pronunciation note: at is a preposition, so fly keeps the stress
entries.русский: накинуться на (с кулаками или с бранью)
entries.separable: no — fly at him, ✗ fly him at. Pronouns follow the preposition.
entries.register: rare — dated in American English; British speakers still use it, and the common relative here is fly into a rage
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a sudden attack, an event (she flew at him before anyone could stand up).
entries.passive: no — ✗ the mailman was flown at by the dog, ✗ the referee was flown at. Say went after him or lunged at him.
entries.see also: fight back, fly by, drive off

entries.meaning: For time to pass very quickly, or for something to pass at speed.
examples: The summer flew by.
Three hours flew by and nobody noticed.
The last two weeks have flown by.
Vacations fly by; Mondays don't.
A motorcycle flew by on the shoulder.

senses.head: Pass quickly, of time
body: The everyday sense, usually about a stretch of time you wanted to keep. (пролетать, о времени)
examples: The summer flew by.
Three hours flew by and nobody noticed.
The last two weeks have flown by.
Vacations fly by; Mondays don't.

senses.head: Rush past
body: Literal, of vehicles and runners. (промчаться мимо)
examples: A motorcycle flew by on the shoulder.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — the summer flew BY
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate. When a place follows, by is a preposition and stays put: flew by the window.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; time passing in sense 1 (the summer flew by), literal speed in sense 2 (a motorcycle flew by on the shoulder).
entries.passive: no — intransitive: ✗ the summer was flown by, ✗ the window was flown by.
entries.see also: fly out, fly at

entries.meaning: To leave by plane, to send someone somewhere by plane, or in baseball, to be put out on a caught fly ball.
examples: We fly out of Newark at six in the morning.
She flew out Sunday and started work Monday.
The company flew two engineers out the same night.
They flew him out to Phoenix for the interview.
He flied out to right field to end the inning.
The cleanup hitter had flied out twice already.

senses.head: Depart by plane
body: No object. (вылететь, улететь)
examples: We fly out of Newark at six in the morning.
She flew out Sunday and started work Monday.

senses.head: Send by plane
body: Of people and supplies dispatched somewhere. (отправить самолётом, доставить по воздуху)
examples: The company flew two engineers out the same night.
They flew him out to Phoenix for the interview.

senses.head: Be out on a caught fly ball
body: Baseball, and the one place where fly becomes regular: flied out. (выбить мяч, пойманный с лёта)
examples: He flied out to right field to end the inning.
The cleanup hitter had flied out twice already.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — flew her OUT
entries.русский: вылететь (самолётом); отправить самолётом; выбить мяч в аут (бейсбол)
entries.separable: yes when someone is sent — fly out a technician / fly a technician out, and with a pronoun it must separate: they flew her out, never ✗ flew out her. In the travel and baseball senses there is no object.
entries.register: everyday — the baseball sense is American, and note that its past tense is flied out, never ✗ flew out
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses; note that the baseball sense is regular — he flied out to right field, never ✗ he flew out to right field.
entries.passive: restricted — only the dispatch sense: two engineers were flown out the same night, he was flown out to Phoenix for the interview. ✗ Newark is flown out of at six, and the baseball sense has no object at all.
entries.see also: fly by, fly at

entries.meaning: To stop thinking about something, or to give up on it as impossible.
examples: I completely forgot about the dentist.
She'd forgotten about the whole argument by Monday.
Forget about the money — just get the car back.
If it rains, you can forget about the game.
Forget about it; they're not going to call.

senses.head: Fail to remember, put out of mind
body: The plain sense. Forget about is warmer and more conversational than bare forget. (забыть о, упустить из виду)
examples: I completely forgot about the dentist.
She'd forgotten about the whole argument by Monday.

senses.head: Give up on, rule out
body: Usually an imperative: stop hoping for that. (выбросить из головы, и думать забудь)
examples: Forget about the money — just get the car back.
If it rains, you can forget about the game.
Forget about it; they're not going to call.

entries.pronunciation note: about is a preposition, so the stress stays on the second syllable of forget
entries.русский: забыть о; выбросить из головы, и думать не сметь
entries.separable: no — forget about the deposit, ✗ forget the deposit about, ✗ forget it about. Pronouns follow the preposition: forget about it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a change of mental state (I completely forgot about the dentist), unlike stative know; sense 2 lives mostly in the imperative.
entries.passive: yes — one of the few prepositional verbs here with a clean passive: the crate had been forgotten about in the basement, the whole argument was forgotten about by Monday.
entries.see also: do away with, fall through, put off

entries.meaning: To push someone out by shutting them out of everything that matters.
examples: The majority owners froze the two founders out.
Big carriers freeze out small competitors with volume pricing.
They didn't fire her; they just froze her out.
He was frozen out of every meeting that mattered.
If you side with him, they'll freeze you out too.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — froze them OUT
entries.separable: yes — freeze out the minority shareholders / freeze the minority shareholders out, and with a pronoun it must separate: freeze them out, never ✗ freeze out them.
entries.register: everyday — common in business writing and in talk about social groups
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a campaign of exclusion carried out over time (they didn't fire her; they just froze her out).
entries.passive: yes — he was frozen out of every meeting that mattered; the two founders were frozen out by the majority owners.
entries.see also: drive out, fall out, shut out

entries.meaning: For a body of water to become covered with ice.
examples: The pond freezes over by early January most years.
The lake froze over twice last winter.
The river hasn't frozen over since 2014.
Wait until it freezes over and you can walk across.
He'll apologize when hell freezes over.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress, on its first syllable — froze OH-ver
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a change of state (the pond freezes over by early January most years).
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is no verbal passive: ✗ the pond was frozen over by the cold. The lake is frozen over is the adjective describing the result, not something done to the lake.
entries.see also: freeze up, freeze out

entries.meaning: To become unable to speak or act, or — of a machine or a pipe — to seize with cold.
examples: She froze up in the middle of the presentation.
He freezes up every time somebody points a camera at him.
If you freeze up on the first question, the rest is harder.
The pipes froze up over the holiday weekend.
The lock had frozen up and the key wouldn't turn.

senses.head: Panic and go blank
body: Of a person under pressure: on stage, in an interview, at the free-throw line. (оцепенеть, растеряться)
examples: She froze up in the middle of the presentation.
He freezes up every time somebody points a camera at him.
If you freeze up on the first question, the rest is harder.

senses.head: Seize with cold
body: Of pipes, locks, and engines. (заклинить, замёрзнуть)
examples: The pipes froze up over the holiday weekend.
The lock had frozen up and the key wouldn't turn.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — froze UP
entries.separable: there is no object, so there is nothing to separate.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a change of state in both senses: a person going blank, a pipe or a lock seizing with cold.
entries.passive: no — intransitive: ✗ the pipes were frozen up by the holiday cold. After be, frozen up is an adjective naming the state, not a passive.
entries.see also: freeze over, fall apart, freeze out
